title: A useless slaughter (1917)
hook: Benedict XV calls the Great War a useless slaughter and proposes peace

segments.voice: Yesterday, Fatima, and children praying the rosary in a jail cell. Your line was pray for peace. Did you name the people of one war? Today, a pope who tried to stop one. Day nine hundred four.

Across Europe, men are living in trenches, and whole villages have been emptied. From the Vatican, a letter goes out, addressed to the leaders of the nations at war. Catholic soldiers fight on both sides, praying to the same God in the same Mass, on opposite sides of the wire. The letter is from Pope Benedict XV. It doesn't bless a side. It names the war for what he thinks it is.
screen: `A LETTER TO THE NATIONS AT WAR.` → `THE SAME MASS, OPPOSITE TRENCHES.` → `NO SIDE BLESSED.`

segments.voice: Read the letter from its words to its fate. First, the phrase. Benedict asked whether the civilized world must become a field of death, and he called the war a useless slaughter. Not glorious, not holy. Useless. Second, the plan. He didn't stop at grief. He proposed terms: that the moral force of right should take the place of the force of arms, that nations reduce their weapons together, that disputes go to arbitration instead of battle, that the seas be free, and that occupied lands be given back. Third, the answer. Governments on both sides turned it down or ignored it, and some accused him of secretly favoring the enemy. The war went on. Fourth, the other work. While the plan failed, the Vatican did what it could beside it: helping find missing soldiers, passing news between prisoners and their families, and sending relief to the hungry. In the Sermon on the Mount, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God." Notice that the line doesn't promise peacemakers success. Benedict XV didn't get his peace. What he left was a plan on paper and a name for the war: useless slaughter, from a pope who would not call it glorious.
screen: `A FIELD OF DEATH.` · `A PLAN FOR PEACE.` · `REJECTED BY BOTH SIDES.` · `PRISONERS, MISSING, HUNGRY.` · then, large: `BLESSED ARE THE PEACEMAKERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for soldiers. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind people in uniform right now, on any side of any conflict. Someone young on watch at night. Someone wounded. Someone who came home and can't sleep. Their families waiting by a phone. If you pray, you can hold them before God, without asking which side they're on. If you don't pray, hold them in your attention and wish them safety and a way home. The bell holds the time.
Inutile strage. Italian for useless slaughter, the phrase remembered from Pope Benedict XV's letter calling the Great War useless and proposing terms for peace.
Your line: useless slaughter. Today, when you hear an argument about winning, ask quietly what it would take to stop instead. Day nine hundred four.

howItsDone: Catholics pray for peace and for those at war in the prayers of the faithful at Mass, and later popes have also appealed for peace; some parishes remember Benedict XV's peace note when they mark the anniversary of the First World War.

fork.setup: you're the pope. Catholics are fighting on both sides of a great war. what do you do?
options: support the side with more Catholics.
call it a useless slaughter and propose terms for peace.
fork.reveal: he wrote to the warring nations with a plan. both sides rejected it, and the war went on.

original.note: Italian: useless slaughter, the phrase from Benedict XV's peace note remembered in Italian.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pope who said war is bad.
what it means: a letter to the warring nations with a concrete plan, calling the war a useless slaughter.
what a scholar hears: the note's plan included shared disarmament and arbitration; the Vatican also traced prisoners and the missing.

sources.ref: peace note to the heads of the belligerent peoples (Dès le début), 1 August 1917

notes: Peace note paraphrased: 'field of death' / 'useless slaughter' (inutile strage; the note's original was in French), moral force of right in place of material force of arms, simultaneous reduction of armaments, arbitration, freedom of the seas, evacuation of occupied territories. Confirm each point and the original-language phrasing for the original game.
'Catholic soldiers fight on both sides' and 'governments call on God for their side' are general history; Keeper may soften under the claims rule.
Rejection by governments on both sides and accusations of partiality: confirm.
Vatican office for prisoners of war and missing persons, and relief: confirm wording.
'Some of his ideas came back later in other people's plans' (e.g. arbitration, disarmament in later proposals): general; Keeper may cut.
howItsDone: 'later popes have also appealed for peace' is general; Keeper may soften.

Editor pass: cut the unsourced claim that this was 'something popes are rarely expected to do in wartime'; cut 'some of his ideas came back later in other people's plans' (teach and trapdoor) and 'the phrase outlived the war' (fork); the overstated 'refused to call a war anything else' ending now reads 'a pope who would not call it glorious'.
